item.title: Pentagon used emergency measure to change voter forms for Americans abroad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration used an emergency measure this summer to change the language of the federal voter-registration form used by U.S. service members abroad and citizens residing outside the country, potentially restricting some eligible American voters abroad from using the application to request their ballots. Advocates for American citizens overseas say the changes will spark confusion among eligible voters abroad and officials within U.S. election offices. They argue the changes effectively disenfranchise some voters abroad, but the Pentagon says the changes are meant to align the form with federal law. More than 2 million Americans living abroad are eligible to cast their ballots in U.S. elections. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Doris Speer, president of the Association of Americans Resident Overseas, said she believes the changes to the form known as the Federal Post Card Application are "an effort to deter the overseas vote, not to legally stop people from voting but to make the process so difficult that you really have to want to vote to get through it. The result will be confusion, chaos and fewer overseas votes." The changes to the form follow the Trump administration's unsuccessful efforts to restrict voting by mail and pass sweeping voter ID legislation. That proposed legislation, the Save America Act, would require Americans to prove their citizenship when registering to vote and show photo ID to vote, and permit the Department of Homeland Security to obtain access to voter rolls. The political stakes of the upcoming midterm election are high for the GOP. Republicans are in danger of losing their majority in the House of Representatives, and Democrats have vowed to step up their investigations into President Donald if they are in the majority. In August, the Pentagon sought emergency approval to make several changes to the Federal Post Card Application, used by U.S. voters abroad to register to vote and request an absentee ballot. The Pentagon did not solicit public feedback on the change, as normally would be a part of the process for a document change of this nature. The Pentagon told The Washington Post in a statement that recent updates were made "to streamline voter identification instructions and ensure alignment with Federal law" but did not detail which federal law. The Pentagon also did not explain what emergency allowed the government to expedite the form changes. In an Aug. 13 letter to the Office of Management and Budget's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs seeking emergency processing to alter the form, Deputy Undersecretary of War for Personnel and Readiness Sean O'Keefe wrote that the changes were necessary because the previous version of the document may have confused "voters about the information they are required to provide under Federal law and their eligibility to use these forms to register and vote." In justifying the emergency, O'Keefe wrote that "the next Federal election is fewer than 90 days away, so there is insufficient time to modify" the forms via the standard process, adding that "public harm is reasonably likely to result if normal clearance procedures and time periods are followed." Elections are typically scheduled years in advance. Tammy Patrick, a longtime elections administrator who serves as the chief program officer at the National Association of Election Officials, and other advocates for U.S. voters overseas say they still don't understand what constituted an emergency in this case. "I don't think there is an actual emergency," Patrick said. "I have not heard from any election officials about anything related to our infrastructure, neither at the state level … nor at any local level, causing any major concern within our hundreds and hundreds of members." Most notably, the new version of the form changes ID requirements and eliminates a checkbox that allows a voter to declare, "I am a US citizen living outside the country, I have never lived in the United States." That category, sometimes referred to as "never resideds," encompasses the adult children of U.S. citizens who have long lived abroad. A 1986 law established federal protections for military and overseas voters. But states determine voter eligibility rules and residence requirements. Currently, "never resideds" are eligible to vote in 37 states based on their parents' previous residence. Along with changes to the form itself, the General Services Administration's website for the newly altered form also states that it "is for absent Uniform Service members, their families, and citizens residing outside the U.S. intending on returning only." Previously, the federal government made no distinction on who was eligible to use the form based on whether an American citizen intended to return to the United States. Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the nonprofit U.S. Vote Foundation, said that changing the form "without an effective public comment process sends a terrible message to the people who have always been part of it: election officials, usability experts, and organizations like ours. That process used to give us a form that supported voter participation and made life easier for election administrators." Speer, with the Association of Americans Resident Overseas, said she isn't interested in mounting a legal fight ahead of the midterm election, arguing that any effort to stop the federal government from using the new form could create even more confusion for voters. But Dzieduszycka-Suinat said U.S. Vote Foundation is "investigating this issue and the emergency process that was used with legal counsel." She said the organization is prepared to fight in court. Eligible "never resided" voters must now seek their ballots through states, rather than through the federal government. California, for example, is one of 37 states that allow a U.S. citizen who never has lived in the United States to vote if their parent or legal guardian was previously registered to vote as a resident of the state. The California secretary of state's office told The Post that the state's online voter-registration application continues to include a category for U.S. citizens who "have never resided in the U.S." Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/pentagon-used-emergency-measure-change-090000846.html

item.title: Religion, drone warfare and a new base: 7 takeaways from Hegseth's speech
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a flurry of announcements during a wide-ranging speech to active-duty officers Wednesday. At the beginning of the address, the Pentagon chief stuck to his bread and butter: culture-war grievances , stripping the “woke” out of the Department of Defense (DOD), bashing the news media for its coverage of the Iran war, and proclaiming the “warrior ethos” has been revived and the U.S. military has been “rebuilt.” But the Defense secretary made several newsy announcements that lean into Hegseth's elevation of faith, create a combatant command, partner the Pentagon with different universities and tease a new domestic military base for which governors will compete. Here are the takeaways from Hegseth’s 52-minute speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia: New combatant command focused on autonomous warfare Hegseth announced the formation of a new four-star combatant command focused on developing autonomous warfare like drones and defense robotics. The Defense secretary said it would have “service-like authorities built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force in the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” with the aim of being operational by Oct. 1 next year. The Autonomous Warfare Command, or “AutoWarCom,” will be initially led by Owen West, a former Marine who is now the director of the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit, and Max Strasiser, a Navy SEAL senior chief. Later, a four-star military leader will be announced. “This command will possess directed manpower, budget, acquisition authorities and create dedicated military career pathways for Officers and Enlisted personnel,” Hegseth said in a Wednesday memo . The new command will test equipment and force designs with “realistic opposition” in exercises and rugged environments to figure out what works on the battlefield, the Defense secretary said in the memo. Project Meridian and warfare's future Hegseth revealed that SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) will lead a new Pentagon effort to study the future of warfare, dubbed Project Meridian. The Pentagon chief said the project is meant to harness America’s innovators, senior leaders and technologists to look decades into the future and “forecast the creative solution for tomorrow’s conflicts.” “It is futuristic on purpose,” he said of the project, which he clarified was not meant to develop new strategies or policies. “We should have the humility to recognize that the best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon,” Hegseth said. “There are obvious biases and risks to asking ourselves to both ask the questions and answer them.” Hegseth said Musk, Luckey and Gingrich, under the leadership of Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, “will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes, without any creative limitations or restrictions, on any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon.” All three men were in attendance at the Pentagon as Hegseth made his announcement, and the Pentagon chief said their first meeting on Project Meridian would happen immediately following the event in a sensitive compartmented information facility in the building. States invited to bid for 'next great American' base Hegseth invited governors to bid for their state to be the home of the “next great American” base. “We’re calling on every governor in the country and adjutant general, every tag across this great republic, to step up to the plate and bring us their best sales pitch,” the Defense secretary said. “If your state wants the honor of hosting 15,000 to 25,000 of America’s great troops, show us why and how you’re going to do it, cutting through the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families,” he said during the speech. Naval Station Everett in Washington state was the most recent base built inside the U.S., opening in the 1990s. The base is home to several guided-missile destroyers and Coast Guard ships. Hegseth said the new base will not be a “soulless government installation,” arguing the Pentagon will “plan out and chart out a dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform.” The Pentagon said the base will be off the commercial grid, featuring independent power generation, autonomous systems and advanced air defenses. “We’re talking hundreds of thousands of acres with organic power generation, modern air defenses, and cutting-edge technology, think a fortress,” the secretary said. Service members will have “first-class barracks, world-class training facilities, and thriving communities with top-tier housing, school, childcare and healthcare for families.” Hegseth directed Dale R. Marks, who is assistant secretary of Defense for energy, installations and environment, to lead the Pentagon’s effort to identify, evaluate, select and prepare an optimal site for the base. “Rapid advancements in disruptive technologies, growing strategic alignment among peer adversaries, and persistent, sophisticated cyber intrusions against critical defense and homeland infrastructure necessitate a modernized, resilient posture,” the Defense secretary said in a Wednesday memo. 'Fortress America' takes bases off civilian grid Another new initiative revealed Wednesday is “Fortress America,” which Hegseth claimed will be “a national insurance policy for the American homeland.” Under Fortress, which stands for “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy Supply and Survivability,” every major military installation in America would generate its own power independent of the civilian grid, according to Hegseth. “If an adversary takes down the grid by cyberattack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark,” he said. The effort also is meant to bring critical supply chains home, including rare earth minerals, specialty metals, semiconductors and propellants “mined in America, refined in America, built in America by American workers.” In addition, the Pentagon would build up strategic reserves of such critical needs as munitions, fuel, medicine and blood “deep enough that if the world's supply lines break — and in a real war, they're going to break — America keeps fighting anyway,” Hegseth said. To accomplish this, Hegseth said the U.S. military is “hardening every installation on American soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones, and we're securing the high ground and the airwaves, our satellites, our spectrum,” claiming that the DOD “will be the insurance policy for the entire nation.” New non-Ivy League partnerships for cadets The Defense secretary also said the Pentagon will partner with five more colleges to broaden the corps of cadets. The military training program, called “America's Corps of Cadets,” will include Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University and Hillsdale College. “We need more officers from academic institutions like our military academies and senior military colleges, and today we're going to make that happen,” Hegseth said. Each school will be a “distinguished military college” and will be expected to “maintain exceptionally high standards of cadet discipline, tactical instruction and military organization,” the Pentagon chief said. Military academies like West Point, Naval Academy and Air Force Academy commission most of the officers into the U.S. armed forces, followed by senior military colleges like Texas A&M and the Citadel. Hegseth’s office will begin implementation within 30 days, and within four months, Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata will transition to become the primary office responsible for the program, according to a Wednesday Pentagon memo . “From the Ivy Leagues to the most liberal arts colleges, our colleges and universities have become anti-American DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] worshipping woke factories. Qualities like grit and courage replaced with political correctness and social justice,” Hegseth said. “God and country traded for Che Guevara and critical theory.” Creates Office of Religious Affairs In his last proclamation, Hegseth declared he will establish the Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon that “will report straight to the top.” “Cutting-edge technology ... new basing and bases ... and a better educational pipeline are still incomplete without the most essential component of our republic: faith,” he told the assembled service members. He said the Defense Department has “a sacred duty” to provide troops with “first-class religious support” wherever they’re sent, bashing past administrations for treating the topic as an afterthought. “Political correctness and secular humanism got a vote. Chaplains did not. Budgets were cut. Resourcing and manpower needs were ignored. Base chapels fell apart,” Hegseth claimed. “Decisions about faith and religion were made by secular careerists in cubicles and lawyers running around with red tape.” Starting Wednesday, the Office of Religious Affairs will have “a direct line to the secretary” and will “protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support,” he said. Hegseth frequently invokes his faith and has declared service members’ spiritual health as “equally important” as their physical and mental health. Earlier this year he revamped the U.S. military’s Chaplain Corps, announcing that the officers will no longer wear their rank insignia, instead displaying insignia that reflects their religious affiliation — part of two major changes to the group. Hegseth defends officer cuts At the start of his speech, Hegseth defended his plan to cut 20 percent of generals and admirals at the Pentagon, arguing the major shake-up was long overdue at the department. “Now the media calls that a purge. I call it accountability and long overdue, and frankly, the bare minimum. As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment,” Hegseth said. “You see, you can't change a culture with the same people who enabled it,” he said. “Personnel is policy at every single level.” The move will impact senior leadership positions across the Army, Navy and the Air Force, coming a year after Hegseth oversaw a 10 percent reduction of general officers. The move comes as he has already fired or pushed out more than two dozen senior military officers across the service branches, personnel changes that have unnerved congressional lawmakers on both sides of the aisle . “You see, last year's speech was not for those generals,” Hegseth said during the speech. “It was for you, the backbone of our force, the current and future leaders on the front lines.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. item.title: Millions of Americans face changes to SNAP benefits beginning today
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
For the many millions of people who receive SNAP, grocery budgets will stretch a little further this month. Starting Oct. 1, the maximum SNAP benefit for a family of four in the 48 contiguous states and D.C. will climb to $1,023 a month. The annual bump is meant to help the roughly 36 million people on the food assistance program keep up with grocery prices. Income limits and deductions are rising, too, which means some families will get additional financial support, and more people could become eligible for help. Here's what's changing and what it could mean for your benefits. How much SNAP support will I receive from Oct. 1? The figures in the table are maximums , and most households actually get less. SNAP expects families to put about 30% of their own income toward food, so it takes 30% of a household's net monthly income and subtracts that from the maximum. For example, a family of four with $1,000 a month in net income would be expected to spend $300 on food. Their benefit would be $1,023 minus $300, or $723 a month. The lower a household's income, the closer it gets to the maximum. Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands each have their own benefit amounts, because groceries there tend to cost more than in the lower 48. Shipping distances and local supply chains push prices up. Hawaii's maximum is falling to $1,655 from $1,689 as USDA phases in a lower food-cost estimate. Alaska splits the state into three zones: Urban, Rural 1 and Rural 2. People in towns and cities in the Urban zone get the lowest maximums, while those in more remote rural communities, where prices are higher, get more. Other factors that affect your SNAP benefits The maximum SNAP benefit isn't the only figure changing in October. All figures below are for the 48 contiguous states and D.C. Where a figure depends on household size, it's for a household of four unless noted. Income limits: $3,575 a month gross (up from $3,483 in 2025) Gross income is your household's total income before deductions, and net is what's left after. Most households must fall under both limits to qualify. Standard deduction: $217 for households of one to three people ($209 in 2025) This amount is subtracted from every household's income before benefits are calculated. Larger households get a higher deduction. Shelter deduction cap: $769 ($744 in 2025) If housing and utility costs eat up more than half your income after other deductions, you can deduct the amount above that 50% threshold, up to this cap. Households with an older or disabled member aren't subject to the cap. Asset limit: $3,000 (unchanged from 2025) This is how much a household can have in savings and other countable assets and still qualify. For households with a member who is 60 or older or disabled, the limit rises to $4,750 (from $4,500 in 2025). Minimum benefit: $25 a month ($24 in 2025) This is the smallest benefit an eligible one- or two-person household can receive. Changes to SNAP While SNAP benefits are increasing from this month, the broader picture is a little more complicated. Government data shows that there are actually millions fewer people receiving SNAP compared to last year. Experts say two changes to SNAP introduced in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025, are having — or are set to have — an impact on the number of SNAP recipients. The first of these changes is expanded work requirements and eligibility cuts enacted under the OBBBA, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP) , a left-leaning think tank. For example, the law raised the age range subject to SNAP's 80-hour-a-month work requirement from 18–54 to 18–64, and removed exemptions that had previously covered veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and young adults recently aged out of foster care. It says that SNAP participation fell by roughly 5 million people, or 12%, between July 2025, when the law was signed, and May 2026. While it acknowledges that participation had started to decline prior to July 2025, the CBPP says the fall in numbers accelerated in almost all states after the OBBBA was signed into law. The second of these factors relates to who pays to run the SNAP program. Under the OBBBA, states will have to cover 75% of SNAP's administrative costs from Oct. 1 — up from 50% previously. USDA estimates the change will shift about $16.9 billion in costs to states over five years. Tim Shaw, director of the Benefits Transformation Initiative at the Aspen Institute's Financial Security Program, warned this could make it harder to access SNAP over time. "Most states knew the 75% administrative cost was coming and budgeted for it. But in the longer term, pressure on budgets will increase and states will have to make tough choices," he told Money Talks News . "States will have less leeway to deliver benefits so there may be fewer technological improvements, longer wait times for call centers and more complications to get SNAP." Furthermore, the OBBBA states will also have to cover part of the benefit costs for the first time from Oct. 2027. This will range from 0% to 15% depending on the scale of each state's error rates. The Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality, a research and policy think tank based in Washington, D.C., is among those to warn that the wider OBBBA changes will mean states face "impossibly high costs—forcing them to cut other programs, raise taxes, reduce SNAP access, or end their SNAP programs altogether." The USDA says it projects that the changes in administrative costs will "have a negligible impact on SNAP benefit spending or SNAP participation." How are SNAP increases calculated? Maximum benefits are tied to the Thrifty Food Plan, a USDA estimate of what it costs to feed a family of four (two adults and two children) a healthy diet on a tight budget. Each June, USDA's Food and Nutrition Administration, formerly the Food and Nutrition Service, works out what that basket of groceries costs at current prices. By law, that June figure sets the maximum SNAP benefits for the fiscal year starting Oct. 1. This year's increase, about 3%, reflects how grocery prices have moved over the past year. item.title: Supreme Court will review Trump admin.'s mandatory immigrant detention policy
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for immigrants as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown . The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation. The case will test a key pillar of the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration agenda . Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending. The high court agreed to hear the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a citizen of Brazil. Authorities say he entered the United States illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016. He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory following his September 2025 arrest. He has never been charged or convicted of a crime, his attorneys said. The court is expected to hear the case in the coming months. President Donald Trump’s administration had urged the high court to take up a different but related case that involves the broader constitutional implications of the new policy. Attorneys from the Republican administration argue the circuits’ split is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law.” They say the nation’s courts have been inundated with thousands of petitions filed by immigrants challenging the government’s legal interpretation. “The result is an unworkable patchwork of inconsistent immigration enforcement, where aliens present without admission are subject to mandatory detention in some circuits but are entitled to bond hearings and often released in others,” lawyers for the administration wrote. The plaintiffs are immigrants represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, which says hundreds of district court judges have joined most circuits in rejecting the Trump administration’s new reading of the statutes. Plaintiffs’ lawyers say the administration is trying to deny bond hearings for immigrants apprehended anywhere in the U.S. — no matter how long they’ve lived in the country — rather than limiting the restriction to noncitizens stopped at the border. “Millions of noncitizens could be affected by the government’s new interpretation,” ACLU attorneys wrote. The Trump administration says its new mandatory detention policy is legal under a 1996 immigration law. The policy change departs from the practices of prior administrations, which typically allowed most noncitizens without criminal records to request a bond hearing if they were arrested away from the border. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court . item.title: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives lethal injection attempt
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Tennessee's only female death row inmate has been taken to the hospital after surviving two doses of lethal injection drugs, her lawyers said. Christa Pike, 50, was alive and snoring loudly after being given two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said. She was subsequently taken to a hospital. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said that he had ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and that another scheduled execution had been paused. Gov. Lee said he did not know what her health status is, and called the failed execution "deeply disturbing." He added. "This is a tragedy. There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn't have happened." In a statement posted on Facebook , Tennessee state Sen. Marsha Blackburn called for a return to the electric chair. "This situation is tragic," she said. "Christa Pike should have been executed long ago. Now, this botched process is extending the pain for the family of Colleen Slemmer. While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly." Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for a killing she committed in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court. Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words. However, Pike remained conscious after the first dose. Nashville Banner reporter Steven Hale said she lifted her head off the gurney at 7.54 p.m. She also reportedly asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville, said Pike was seen pointing at her arm and asking, "Does this happen like that?" By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered. Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area. Christa Pike, pictured in January 2023. Tennessee Department of Correction via AP Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper, "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution. "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy." Gov. Lee said he had paused another execution scheduled for Dec. 3 this year. "Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the state's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," he said. Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled." Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said. "I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," Gessner said. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg." The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office." The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set. Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court. Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus. Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001. How common are botched executions? According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI), there have been 64 well-known botched execution attempts between 1982 and the first half of 2026 across the U.S. Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. It acknowledges that the number is an approximation. It has listed the individual cases on its website. Of those 64, the DPI says seven execution attempts resulted in failure. It said the execution of Tennessee inmate Tony Carruthers — which failed when staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug — was the most recent it had documented before Pike. The DPI, which says it does not take a position on the death penalty itself but is critical of problems in its application, cites figures showing that, historically, around 3% of attempted executions between 1890 and 2010 were flawed. Lethal injection has drawn particular scrutiny, with 7.2% of attempted executions being botched, the DPI said, compared with the rate of 3.15% across all methods, including electrocution, hanging and gas. Experts have pointed to difficulties establishing intravenous lines, questions about the drugs used and the ethical role doctors can play in executions , since their ethics code requires them to swear to preserve life. Such figures on botched executions have been questioned by some, including Michael Conklin, an assistant professor of business law at Texas A&M University–Central Texas. In a 2020 paper , he argued that some of the cases classified as botched attempts included those in which the prisoner resisted, those in which there were difficulties inserting the IV, and those in which prison officials opened the curtain too early. The state of Tennessee has experienced recent issues that predate Pike's case. In April 2022, Gov. Lee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022. Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug, pentobarbital. Tony Carruthers was scheduled to be executed on May 21, 2026. Tennessee Department of Correction via AP Pike's failed execution was Tennessee's second this year . Carruthers, who was convicted of the kidnapping and murders of three people in Memphis, was scheduled to be executed on May 21, 2026, but officials abandoned the attempt after they were unable to establish the intravenous access needed to administer the drug. The ACLU , which was part of his legal team, said witnesses reported more than an hour of attempts to establish a line while Carruthers groaned in pain. Families of victims, however, may feel differently. The family of Slemmer, Pike's victim, traveled to Nashville expecting to witness the execution. Her mother, May Martinez, told the Associated Press she had waited decades to see it happen, "Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," she said. There were 47 executions in 2025 , according to the DPI, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman , who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black , who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead. item.title: Trump says he regrets appointing Gorsuch, Barrett and Kavanaugh to Supreme Court
item.description:

item.title: Pennsylvania reports its 5th measles-related death of the year amid outbreak
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A Parkside Pediatrics provider assessing a patient with measles symptoms in Spartanburg, South Carolina, on 30 January 2026. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Pennsylvania has reported its fifth measles-associated death of 2026 as the state’s ongoing outbreak climbs to 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The Pennsylvania department of health said on Wednesday that an unvaccinated Lancaster county resident who tested positive for measles had died. Health officials did not release further information about the individual, citing privacy protections. The death marks the fifth Pennsylvania resident to meet the state’s definition of a measles-associated death this year after a fourth death two weeks ago. Due to how the Trump administration has changed its method for reporting measles deaths, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has not counted the Pennsylvania measles deaths in its national tally . As of Monday 28 September, Pennsylvania had recorded 40 new positive cases. The outbreak has now reached 39 counties, with 943 cumulative confirmed cases, 176 hospitalizations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths. Only four of those confirmed cases have involved vaccinated individuals, representing less than 1% of the state’s total cases. Health officials say daily totals can change, but monitoring the numbers gives residents and healthcare providers a clearer picture of community transmission across Pennsylvania and helps guide the state’s response. Agricultural communities in Lancaster and Mifflin counties have remained at the center of Pennsylvania’s outbreak. Utah, Florida, Virginia and Texas have also reported dozens of cases, according to tracking from Johns Hopkins University. Since the outbreak began in late April, staff at state health centers have administered more than 5,500 measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) vaccinations through 180 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities, according to a statement released on Wednesday. Dozens of additional vaccination clinics are planned for the coming weeks and months, depending on community interest and need, the statement added. More than 3,600 measles cases have been reported across the US in 2026, according to the CDC. The US eliminated measles in 2000, though it is unclear whether it can retain that status amid the recent outbreaks. Measles is considered one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. The MMR vaccine prevents 97% of measles cases. Vaccination rates among kindergarten-aged children, which are considered an important indicator, have slowly declined as experts argue the Trump administration is promoting confusion and misinformation about vaccines among parents. Earlier this month, Pennsylvania requested emergency assistance from the CDC in response to the measles outbreak, but warned that the request could be withdrawn unless the federal agency publicly recognized the measles-associated deaths reported by the state. The dispute began after Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary and former head of an anti-vaccine advocacy group, publicly questioned whether the deaths linked to the measles outbreaks since he took office were caused by the virus or by another condition. item.title: Early voting data shows emerging signs of a Democratic advantage in the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
"I Voted" stickers sit on a table at Naperville Municipal Center in Naperville, Illinois, on September 24, 2026, on the first day of early voting ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. - Kamil Krzaczyski/AFP/Getty Images Election Day is still a month away, but more than 700,000 Americans have already voted across at least 30 states. There are signs emerging of the advantage Democrats have in motivating their voters – a trend that’s played out in polling all summer long. In several states with key Senate or governor races this fall, Democrats make up a larger share of voters requesting ballots so far than they did at this point in 2024. In Iowa, Democrats have made 67% of ballot requests, up from 54% at this point in 2024. In Pennsylvania, it’s 66%, up from 62%, and in Maine it’s 57%, up from 53%. And according to data from the North Carolina State Board of Elections, 42% of ballot requests are from Democrats, up from 36% at this point two years ago. It’s worth noting that in all of those states except for Iowa, ballot requests at this point in 2022 were more Democratic than they are now. The uptick in the share of requests from Democrats would be in line with polling, special election results and primary turnout, all of which have indicated Democrats may be more motivated to vote this November. On the other hand, it could just be further evidence of Republicans continuing to shift to preferring other forms of voting. An important caveat: While the fact that a person has voted is generally public information, your ballot itself is secret, so this data can’t tell us how many votes a party or candidate has won. That won’t be known until states start reporting results after the polls close on November 3. Early voting data also only shows one slice of voters: a slice that is typically older and less Republican than the electorate as a whole. Early voters are skewing older Voting patterns have shifted in the last several years as the country has emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic. As mail voting has fallen from its 2020 highs, voters 65 and older have made up a larger share of people choosing to vote that way, going from 27% of mail voters in 2020 to 31% in 2022 and 37% in 2024, according to CNN Exit Poll data. That’s not unexpected. Mail voting can be a convenient option for older people who might have trouble getting to the polls. In many states where voters need an excuse to vote by mail, age itself can qualify as a reason to receive a mail-in ballot. There are early signs that that trend is continuing this year. In nearly every state for which there is comparable data, voters 65 and older make up a larger share of ballot requests this year than they did at this point in either 2022 or 2024. A big Democratic advantage in Virginia Perhaps the most positive signs for Democrats so far come from Virginia, which has reported both by far the most total votes of any state in CNN’s count and is the only state which has reported substantial numbers of both early in-person and mail votes. While Virginia voters don’t register by party, there’s a clear relationship between how a locality voted in 2024 and its relative pace of early voting. Cities and counties that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 20 percentage points are at 78% of their turnout from this time in 2024, while those that voted for President Donald Trump by 20 points are at just 61%. Partisan turnout, as measured by the share of voters who have only participated in one party’s primaries since 2022, also points to a considerable Democratic advantage in the early voting period relative to the same point in 2024. While the turnout so far shows a clear advantage in Democratic motivation, Republican voters could close the gap as Election Day nears. It’s still early in the voting period – Virginians cast over 4.5 million votes in 2024 and over 3.4 million votes in 2025. The Senate race in Virginia is not expected to be competitive this year, and Republican voters may be more motivated in more highly contested races. Still, two competitive House races in the state also suggest a move towards Democrats in terms of enthusiasm. Democratic primary participants outnumber Republican primary participants by 15 points among votes cast so far in the 1st District and 18 points in the 2nd District. Both districts are battlegrounds currently represented by Republicans facing tough challengers: Rep. Rob Wittman in the 1st and Rep. Jen Kiggans in the 2nd. At the same point in 2024, the partisan composition was relatively split in both districts, with Republican primary voters leading by about 3 points in the 1st District and Democratic primary voters leading by 2 points in the 2nd District. Statewide, Democratic primary participants outpace Republicans by about 18 points, up from 8 points at the same point in 2024. Early voting data has its limits Data on pre-election voting is valuable but it does have limits. Early vote data is compiled by CNN, the Associated Press, and the data firm Catalist, a company that provides data, analytics and other services to Democrats, academics and nonprofit advocacy groups, including insights into who is voting before November. The number of votes cast so far is a tiny fraction of the roughly 57 million pre-election votes cast in 2022 and an even smaller share of the roughly 112 million votes cast overall in that election but is expected to grow substantially over the next few weeks. The data so far is also largely limited to mail ballots, as very few states have started significant early in-person voting. In recent years mail voters have been much more Democratic, while early in-person voters have been more evenly split or Republican leaning. This story has been updated with additional information. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/politics/cnn-early-voting-takeaways-democratic-advantage

item.title: LSU student says she was raped by a football player who is still on the team
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
LSU's Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, La. (Stacy Revere / Getty Images file) A Louisiana State University student who claims a school football player raped her last year is speaking out about how the school handled her report and the lack of guidance she said she received throughout the process. Kendall Danielle Francis talked on TikTok about the monthslong Title IX investigation that played out after she reported the October rape to the school. Two days into the current semester, she said, she received an email while she was in class to notify her that the student, who had been suspended for two semesters, had his punishment modified upon appeal to four semesters’ probation. He would remain on campus and could continue to play football, she said. “Now I am just trying to speak on my story, because LSU does really protect their athletes, especially their football players,” Francis, who was 18 at the time of the alleged incident, said in the Sept. 14 social media post. As a result of the student’s remaining on campus, Francis said, she moved her classes online. Francis wasn’t aware that filing the Title IX complaint was a separate process from filing criminal charges, a spokesperson for Francis said Wednesday. “When she filed for Title IX, they [the university] did not tell her she could also contact the police and have them launch a criminal investigation,” a spokesperson said. “She just assumed LSU would do the criminal investigation.” Francis’ post, however, caught the attention of East Baton Rouge Parish District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose office announced it was launching a criminal investigation. He has requested “all reports, interviews, evidence, and other relevant records” from LSU, the university police and the Baton Rouge Police Department, as well as the coroner’s office, which handles the evidence collection from sexual assault victims. “This is now an open criminal investigation,” Moore said Sept. 22 in a statement on his agency’s Facebook page . Francis’ allegations come as accusations that members of a fraternity gang-raped a female Cornell University student for several hours have renewed questions nationwide about whether universities are doing enough to protect students from sexual assault. LSU President Wade Rousse said in a statement that the university is cooperating with investigators. “Let me assure everyone that this incident has been handled professionally and that LSU has strictly followed our policies, procedures and best practices, including the Title IX process, to guide our actions to date,” Rousse said. Title IX is a federal law that requires all universities that receive federal funds to put safeguards in place to protect students from sexual predators. Francis didn’t respond to several reach-outs from NBC News to discuss her online allegations or share the findings of the Title IX investigation. In her TikTok video , Francis said she was assaulted at around 4:30 a.m. Oct. 18 “by a football player at LSU.” “That day basically changed my life,” she said, adding that she “developed pretty severe anxiety” and that after an official diagnosis she began taking medication to manage it. Francis said that she was taken to the hospital, where she had “a rape kit done,” but that she didn’t initially press charges. “However, I did go through the Title IX process here at LSU, which took a really, really long time,” she said. Francis said she returned to school assuming the football player was suspended and under investigation by the police. She said she was in a class when she was notified via email that the alleged attacker was still “accountable” for the rape and would be on probation and allowed to attend classes on campus and play football. “I was under the impression that because LSU found him responsible that LSU would do their part, that criminal charges, you know, would be pursued,” Francis said in an interview last week with WAFB-TV of Baton Rouge . Universities are generally not required to automatically alert the police when a Title IX sexual assault or rape investigation is underway, especially if the survivor requests confidentiality or chooses not to involve law enforcement. Francis said in a second TikTok post that she reported the alleged rape this month to LSU police in an attempt to press charges. NBC News has reached out to the agency to confirm that, but so far there has been no response. The Baton Rouge-based newspaper The Advocate reported that it had obtained the Title IX documents from the case and that they confirm Francis’ assertion that the football player was found responsible for the rape. Those documents, according to the newspaper, also confirm that his punishment was reduced on appeal from a two-semester suspension to four semesters of probation. Some of the sexual activity between Francis and the football player was consensual, according to those documents as reported by The Advocate. Still, the football player admitted that he didn’t specifically ask for Francis’ consent before they had intercourse “and did not stop when he later asked and she was silent,” according to the Title IX documents. Meg Casper Sunstrom, an LSU spokesperson, didn’t confirm the outcome of the Title IX proceedings or the discipline that was handed down to the student. Nor did she respond to questions about whether the football player was at LSU and playing for the team. “Since there was no criminal complaint filed by the victim, LSU appropriately turned the issue over to our Title IX office as mandated by law,” Sunstrom said in an email. But she noted that the football player did “self-report” an incident involving his accuser with the LSU Police Department. Dated Oct. 18, 2025, the report, obtained from LSU via a public records request, said the 19-year-old football player was at the school’s football facility when he called police “due to concerns about potential accusations from the other party.” The report gave no indication what those potential accusations were. The incident report says the football player told police that Francis had told him she was mentally unwell and had “thoughts of suicidal ideation.” The responding officer noted in the report that police had been in touch with Francis four days earlier, on Oct. 14, “regarding a similar incident.” An officer determined that Francis posed no danger to herself and “seemed to be commenting out of spite.” This time, the report says, when police went to Francis’ on-campus residence, “it was evident that Francis’s mental state was unstable.” The report doesn’t detail the basis for that conclusion. “She agreed to go to the hospital for further evaluation, and I transported her to Baton Rouge General Hospital for assessment,” the responding officer wrote in his report. Francis said in her TikTok post that she dreads the possibility of running into her alleged attacker on campus. “So that made my anxiety really, really bad, because I don’t want to face this person,” she said. “I really just wanted to bring awareness upon this situation, because I’m just dealing with a lot right now, and I think that this story needs to be heard.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/lsu-student-says-was-raped-football-player-still-team-rcna600539

item.title: FCC chair says government-funded Trump ads ‘don’t raise any red flags’
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr has been a staunch defender of President Donald Trump and gone after some of his critics. (Al Drago / Getty Images file) Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr said Wednesday that new pro-Trump TV ads paid for with government funds don’t “merit any sort of FCC review.” “It doesn’t strike me as anything at all out of the ordinary,” Carr said of the ads, which have aired across the country in recent weeks. Asked about allegations that the ads are “propaganda,” Carr laughed. The White House has “explained that these are just normal-course public service announcements, PSAs, that you see all the time. I don’t think there’s anything unique or different about it,” he said at a news conference . “There’s nothing in there that strikes me that merit any sort of FCC review,” said Carr, whom Trump appointed to the agency. A reporter pointed out that the progressive advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC noting that the Trump campaign used one of the ads in 2024. Carr brushed off the concern, telling reporters that “there’s groups on the left that have, you know, long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process” but that the ads “don’t raise any red flags.” Public Citizen did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC, told NBC News in a statement, “I recognize the concern shared by others that taxpayer dollars are being used to promote a political message, particularly given the timing of these ads coming so close to an election.” “While it is not surprising to see the FCC exercise a double standard when it comes to its investigative decisions, I am certain we will hear more about this from folks in Congress, who are ultimately responsible,” her statement said. The use of federal funds to pay for the ads has drawn bipartisan criticism , with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., saying they “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars” and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., calling them an “absolute violation of what democracy is supposed to look like.” Trump defended the ads when asked about them Wednesday in the Oval Office. “I’m not running for office and I don’t talk about anybody,” he said. “When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.” “Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country,” he added. The first of the ads features Trump describing how he wants to “defeat communism” while the song “ Love Me ” by JMSN plays in the background. Another spot is a slightly shorter version of a 2024 Trump campaign ad, which shows him walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voice-over to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.” In its complaint Tuesday, Public Citizen said that the messages are thinly veiled campaign ads timed to motivate Trump’s supporters ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and that they are unlawful. “Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising. Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads,” the complaint says, adding that none of the ads to date “meet the standard of a public service announcement.” “They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program,” the complaint says. Carr has made headlines for using his post to go after late-night comedians like Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel and network programs that he has alleged have liberal biases. The FCC issued an order this year directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated television stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule after the White House and ABC clashed over a joke Kimmel made about first lady Melania Trump. Disney is challenging the review with a suit alleging the FCC is seeking to coerce and retaliate against “a network that refuses to bow to the ⁠administration’s ​demands.” Carr has said the ABC license review stems from the FCC’s probe of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices — not “speech.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/fcc-brendan-carr-says-government-funded-trump-ads-dont-raise-red-flags-rcna600724

item.title: Flydubai pilot hailed a hero after fighting off attacker as plane plunged
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for saving passengers after he was stabbed by his colleague in an alleged attempt to crash a Flydubai plane on Wednesday. - Israel Foreign Ministry/Reuters The Indian pilot who fought off a savage attack by his copilot and helped prevent an apparent hijack of a Flydubai plane heading to Israel with more than 170 people on board is being hailed as a hero. Captain Smit Machchhar was stabbed while trying to fend off the attacker, leaving him badly wounded. During the struggle the cockpit door was opened, allowing other passengers to rush in, subdue his assailant, and take control of the plane that was enroute to Tel Aviv. Machchhar’s actions have received widespread praise from political leaders, passengers who were onboard, those who know him as well as strangers who gathered in his home town to celebrate his bravery. Kaushik Gandhi, who lives in the same building as Machchhar’s parents, told CNN the pilot was always smiling and happy, a real “gentleman.” He described Machchhar as “first class” and said he would always say hello when visiting. “Our entire India should be proud … he has brought glory to India’s name everywhere in the world,” Gandhi told CNN, adding he was “thumping (his) chest” in pride. A crowd of supporters have also gathered in Ghatkopar East, the eastern Mumbai suburb where Machchhar’s family lives. They were waving Indian flags and photos of the hero pilot. “It is a very precious moment and proud moment for a country like us that we have been through, you know, lot of hustles,” Rahul Pandey, one of those gathered there, told CNN. “Smit Machchhar is a talented, soft spoken, kind-hearted and a person with good nature,” said Jinat Shah, who used to live next door to him in Mumbai before the pilot moved to Dubai. “He is an incredible person, and I hope for his fast recovery,” Shah told Indian news agency ANI. Passengers who were on flight FZ1073 described those chaotic moments , during which the plane plummeted 17,400 feet in less than 120 seconds. One told CNN: “I was just sure I was going to die.” But after the attacker was restrained, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where it was safely landed by two standby pilots who happened to be flying as passengers unknown content item - Machchhar, who is reported to be a 39-year-old father of two, was seriously wounded in the attack. Images show showed a gruesome scene onboard following the attack, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask. Machchhar had suffered “massive blood loss” and was “severely wounded,” dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, told CNN. “I think that if we had waited even a few more moments, we would have lost him; his blood pressure had plummeted, he suddenly lost consciousness, and there was blood everywhere,” he said. His bravery “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN. Machchhar has received medical care at a hospital in Saudi Arabia, according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh, and was then transported to the United Arab Emirates. Parag Shah, who represents Ghatkopar East, the eastern Mumbai suburb Machchhar is from, told CNN that the pilot was “out of danger” after undergoing surgery on Wednesday, citing family members. He said Machchhar’s parents traveled to Dubai to be with him. A plane carrying passengers from an earlier Flydubai flight that was diverted to Saudi Arabia arrives at Ben Gurion Airport on September 30, 2026 in Tzafria, Israel. - Erik Marmor/Getty Images Celebrated as a hero Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn’t Machchhar’s “childhood dream,” he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025. Initially, he’d enrolled in a textile engineering course after school. “I finished the entire course, I still was young so wanted to (do) a little more studies,” he said. Once he decided on flying, training took him to New Zealand, where he arrived aged around 19, in the southern city of Dunedin. “He was always sort of a jovial young man and he tried hard,” his instructor at the time Philip Kean told CNN. In a group photograph Kean shared from those days, Machchhar is easy to pick out. “He definitely got a smile of his own… he’s sort of a happy, happy chap,” said Kean, CEO of Mainland Air in Dunedin. This picture blurred by CNN shows Smit Machchhar when he was training to be a pilot in New Zealand around 2008. - Mainland Air Before joining Flydubai, Machchhar spent 11 years with Indian carrier SpiceJet, rising to the position of Senior Commander, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before Wednesday’s incident, one of the most unusual situations he had faced during his over 15 years of flying was the birth of a baby on board. A woman on the plane, who was not at term, had started experiencing labor pains, Machchhar told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast. “Within 7-10 minutes, she was like, ‘captain this is now advancing toward a delivery.’” Machchhar said he and the first officer started to check for the nearest airfields and conditions to make a safe landing. “Both the mother baby were fine,” he added. Watching the news of Machchhar’s heroic actions on the Flydubai flight from New Zealand, his former instructor Kean was full of praise for the young man he had once taught. “It was an amazing feat,” he told CNN. “There could have been a whole airplane load of people wiped out in a matter of seconds, and luckily they got the door open… luckily he could hang on and save the day. Another half a minute would have been all over.” “I’m very proud,” he said. “I’m very proud that he handled that situation… It’s great the way it turned out.” Machchhar has become a national hero for two nations –– Israel, where most of the passengers hailed from, and his own home country, India. “The pilot from Mumbai who proved to be a hero,” wrote the Times of India. “Viewers, if 166 Israelis go home tonight without a scratch, it is all down to the bravery of one single Indian, Captain Smit Machchhar,” a CNN News-18 anchor said during his primetime program. Speaking on the podcast last year how he felt to be a pilot, Machchhar’s answer was simple: “Blessed.” Additional reporting by Sandi Sidhu. item.title: Ex-Arizona frat leader gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
item.description:

Flagstaff — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail Wednesday for his role in a hazing that led to the death of a pledge. Carter Eslick, 20, also received three years of supervised probation during a sentencing hearing in Coconino County Superior Court. Eslick had pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, at an off-campus house. An autopsy found Martinez died of alcohol poisoning with a blood-alcohol content of 0.425% — more than five times the state's legal limit for drivers 21 and over. Martinez was among four Delta Tau Delta pledges who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez's sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said. Martinez's parents appeared remotely in court, still grieving their son, and said they want accountability and reform within Greek life, CBS Phoenix affiliate KPHO-TV reported . Eslick was the fraternity's pledge master at the time and was responsible for welcoming new members. The hearing began with testimony from five of Eslick's friends and family members who attested to his character while warning about the dangers of fraternity culture, KPHO noted. "While trying to teach my children these things, I realized I failed to teach him or explain to them, and in those gaps, toxic influence and toxic communities have stepped in," said Cody Eslick, Carter's father. Carter Eslick apologized to Martinez's family, KPHO said. "I am so incredibly deeply sorry for the events that happened on Jan. 31, and I take full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual," Eslick said. "And if I had known that one day somebody's life could be in my hands, there is no way in hell I would have ever looked that way." Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said no sentence can undo the harm to the Martinez family. "My hope is that this case helps people understand the serious dangers of hazing and encourages them to speak up and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss," Barker said in a statement. Judge Stacy Krueger said Eslick knew what he did was dangerous and was troubled that no one spoke out against it. Eslick could face additional jail time if he doesn't meet the conditions of probation, which include creating and delivering 305 anti-hazing presentations and keeping the court updated on his progress. He also can't use alcohol or drugs unless prescribed. The university suspended the fraternity after Martinez's death, and the national organization later closed the NAU chapter. She was married to actor Doug Hutchison - known for roles in The Green Mile, A Time to Kill and I Am Sam - in 2011, spurring headlines internationally over the controversy and appearances on several reality programmes in the US, including the VH1 series Couples Therapy. Other survivors of child marriage also applauded the new law. "California has sent a clear message to the world today," Brittany Bee, a former child bride, told the BBC. "A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path." Bee told the BBC she was wed at the age of 17 to escape an abusive home - only to then be allegedly abused by her adult husband. "I was just going from one prison to another," she explained. "People have the audacity to tell me that I made a choice - kids, they can't consent." Bee and other child marriage survivors have been working for years to have child marriages banned in California and across the United States. About a decade ago, the practice was still allowed across all US state but more and more states have been altering laws. California is the 18th to ban it since 2018. In the state, there had been no legal age to wed, allowing children to get married as long as their parents consent and a judge signs off on the nuptials. There was also no mechanism for people under 18 to get divorced and many girls say they were trapped in abusive and predatory relationships. Unchained At Last, an advocacy group fighting to end child marriage across the US, said about 9,000 girls were wed each year in California and that almost all child marriages involved girls to adult men. Advocates say that many in the US don't even know that child marriage is legal in so many US states, nor that is has led to allegations of abuse. Sara Tasneem, who says she was forced to marry a man nearly twice her age when she was 15 years old, told the BBC that it felt "surreal" to finally have the state recognise that child marriage should be banned. She says she started lobbying for this herself in 2017. She was introduced to her husband the morning of their arranged marriage. "I was forced to be his wife and that day, my entire life changed," she told the BBC. She became a mother the following year, at the age of 16, and dropped out of school. "To have seen the arc of this bill come to fruition has been a marathon," Tasneem said. "I'm just grateful that kids cannot get married after January 1, 2027 in California." item.title: Cornell report details student's 'I felt like bait' testimony in rape case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
During a 2025 hearing at Cornell University, an unidentified female former student who alleges she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024 described her harrowing night at the house surrounded by multiple men: "I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in." Her description is included in a heavily-redacted 99-page report, obtained by ABC News, that was prepared by the university last year as it investigated what happened. As part of its investigation, Cornell conducted 50 interviews with 32 witnesses, including the fraternity brothers Jane Doe accused in a civil lawsuit filed earlier this month of gang rape, and determined that someone at the Chi Phi house had overdosed on ketamine one day prior to Jane Doe's experience. ABC News - PHOTO: This photo shows the former Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, where a former Cornell University student alleges that she was drugged and gang-raped in 2024. "Ketamine was a substance used by multiple individuals in the Chi Phi house at the time, including [redacted] who had overdosed on or about October 18, 2024," the report said. Jane Doe told investigators the ketamine she took that night induced a "vague consciousness" that left her disoriented. "So, lights are on, but nobody's home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level," Doe said, according to the report. "I know it sounds super weird to say. I know it happened, but I don't remember it." The investigators also noted an apology from one of the fraternity brothers during the hearing. "I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," said the fraternity brother, who Cornell's investigation concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation." "And that I'm sorry I couldn't tell if she was under the influence ... just sorry that I felt like if something actually bad happened, I didn't stop it." University agrees to independent investigation, governor says Earlier Wednesday, Cornell University agreed to initiate an independent investigation into how the Ivy League school handled the allegations, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul told ABC News. Hochul called for the outside review , saying the allegations raised "serious questions about Cornell campus culture" and whether the university is doing all it can to protect students. Spencer Platt/Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this Feb. 10, 2026, file photo, New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks to the media in New York. "I wanted to make sure they knew how important this was, and they absolutely agreed. And they're acting on this this afternoon. So, they'll be reporting on what the details are, but they will be conducting what I asked for, which is an independent outside investigation of what happened," Hochul told ABC News on Wednesday. "People need to know the truth and I think it's important for the public, for the victim, her family and the university community to know that their university did everything that they're supposed to do," she said. New York Gov. Hochul calls for 'transparent, independent review' of Cornell response to alleged group rape Cornell's internal data show 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing sexual assault during their time on campus, but Hochul said the problem was acute on every campus. "There's been a culture of this kind of treatment of young women on campuses for as long as I've been in college, and it has to change," Hochul said. Cornell confirmed the outside investigation on Wednesday but has not yet provided details. Prosecutors in central New York this week announced that they are reopening the investigation of the alleged sexual assault after the former student filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged, assaulted and gang raped by seven former and current members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell, sparking outrage about the incident. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said in a statement that his office is considering whether to bring criminal charges related to the incident, though he said the allegations in the civil complaint are "dramatically different" than the woman's statement to police two years ago. In an interview with ABC News , Van Houten acknowledged that he relied on the investigation conducted by Cornell Police and said his office didn't "independently investigate" the allegations. Cornell's Chi Phi chapter is barred from campus. Trey Robb, the interim executive director of Chi Phi fraternity, said in a statement that all the accused members were kicked out of the Cornell chapter within three days of Jane Doe filing her police report in 2024. 35% of Cornell undergraduate women reported having been sexually assaulted: Survey Three of the defendants named in the suit have denied the allegations through their attorneys. "Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Cornell said in a statement Monday, in part. In an earlier statement, Cornell said it conducted a thorough Title IX investigation of Jane Doe's allegations. "At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell," the university's statement said. Cornell did not specify who was disciplined, how many and for what. The university said the investigation was conducted over several months and included hearings before a panel of trained faculty and staff. Text messages between Jane Doe and fraternity member unearthed A report prepared by Cornell as part of its investigation into the sexual assault allegations included text messages between the Jane Doe and one of the people she accused of rape -- the fraternity member who had invited her to the Chi Phi house. According to the text messages, which were obtained by ABC News, Jane Doe told the man four days after the alleged incident that "everyone knows" and "my reputation is destroyed and I'm utterly ashamed." In the Oct. 23, 2024, exchange Jane Doe texted the man, later identified by the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office as Male Number 1: "everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex and s--- is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common,, I'm also really open minded tho, I luv you king." Cornell student who made rape allegations said sexual encounters 'felt like coercion' in 2024 statement On Nov. 7, 2024, when Male Number 1 expressed concern that he was "being labeled an assaulter," Jane Doe replied, "I haven't said anything but I do know people are changing the narrative because like in any sexual scenario w one woman and many men the woman was probably the victim." "I know there are rumors I was gang banged," her text continued. On Nov. 8, 2024, Male Number 1 asked Jane Doe for a phone call. She replied, "I think I'm done talking to you. I know you lied." It's not clear from the text messages what Jane Doe was referring to but Male Number 1 responded, "What? Can you call?" Jane Doe answered, "no. never again." A week later, Jane Doe gave a sworn statement to Cornell University police. She described that she felt incapacitated, saying she declined to participate in some of the sexual activity and that the incidents at Chi Phi fraternity house "felt like coercion," according to a copy of the police report obtained by ABC News.
